paras: The attempted lynching of Ed Anderson took place near Oakley and Madisonville, outside Cincinnati, Ohio, in August 1881, when residents hunting two Black men accused of highway robbery caught Anderson and nearly lynched him. His companion escaped after about a hundred shots were fired at him, and Anderson was held as a prisoner. The capture ran as a wire item from Utah to Arizona, while only an Ohio weekly reported the near-lynching.

According to a Cincinnati dispatch of August 8, two Black men had been causing "a reign of terror" around Oakley and Madisonville over the previous two or three nights. They were accused of assaulting and robbing half a dozen people and of shooting and wounding two or three of them. The Eaton Democrat later said their acts had become "so bold and notorious" that the neighborhood turned out in full force.

On August 8 citizens were reported to have the two men surrounded in the woods and to expect their capture. One of them, who gave his name as Ed Anderson, was caught in a cornfield near Mount Pleasant. The other escaped "for the time," but only after about one hundred shots had been fired at him in the dark.

A Cincinnati dispatch of August 9 said Anderson had been identified as one of the robbers and that a watch found on him was the one stolen the previous Friday night from Frank Henderson, son of John Henderson. According to the Eaton Democrat, it was "with difficulty" that the prisoner was kept from being lynched; the paper did not say who protected him or where he was held.
No report of a hearing, trial or the companion's capture appears in the coverage.

The Chicago Tribune ran the first report under the heading "Lawless Negroes," and a shorter wire calling the men "desperado negroes" who had been "corraled" appeared in the Salt Lake Herald, the Helena Weekly Herald and the Benton Weekly Record. The capture wire, headed "Highway Robber Captured" in the Las Vegas Daily Gazette, ran in the Memphis Daily Appeal, the Daily Los Angeles Herald and the Arizona Weekly Citizen. None of these items mentioned the threat to lynch Anderson, which appeared only in a one-paragraph item in the Eaton Democrat's "Ohio State News" column on August 18.
Every report took the robbery accusations as fact and gave the men's race in its first line, and the one paper that reported the threat did not comment on it.

Printings of the capture wire placed Oakley and Madisonville "north of this city" in Memphis and Las Vegas but "south of this city" in Los Angeles and Arizona. The Helena and Benton papers said the Cincinnati Commercial had raised penny subscriptions "for their capture," but the Salt Lake Herald printed the subscriptions as a separate item, "for Captain Cook."

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Ed Anderson
bases: Citizens hunted two Black men accused of highway robbery, fired about a hundred shots at one and, by the Eaton Democrat's account, were kept 'with difficulty' from lynching the captured Ed Anderson (A2, A3, A9).

No one was reported killed: Anderson was held as a prisoner and his companion escaped (A3, A9). The neighborhood that turned out in force made an attempt the papers describe as a near-lynching, without lawful authority, over an accusation of robbery (A9).

A Chicago Tribune dispatch, a wire on the capture and the Eaton Democrat's Ohio summary agree on the manhunt and Anderson's capture (A2, A3, A9); the attempt to lynch him appears only in the Eaton Democrat (A9).

framing.detail: Western papers ran the corraling and capture wires under heads such as 'Desperadoes Corraled' and 'Highway Robber Captured', treating the accusations as fact.
The Chicago Tribune headed its dispatch 'Lawless Negroes' and the Eaton Democrat reported the near-lynching in one line without comment.
